name: Manganese toxicity / high-manganese response
summary: A measurement- and exposure-dependent Cannabis differential with conflicting visual descriptions. One controlled T1 study reported older-leaf marginal chlorosis progressing inward, a field survey described interveinal yellowing and necrosis, and a later pH-by-micronutrient study produced a cultivar-dependent lower-leaf response only under combined extreme conditions. No pattern supports image- or video-only confirmation.
affectedParts: lower and older fan leaves in the controlled T1 sequence
interveinal tissue in field diagnostic observations
midrib-adjacent tissue during advanced controlled injury
most-recently-mature leaves for standardized tissue analysis
upper, middle, and lower canopy for distribution mapping
source water, fertilizer, substrate, and root zone for exposure confirmation
stages: any stage only as an analytically unresolved differential
indicators: In one controlled Cannabis sativa T1 study, lower or older leaf margins became yellow after seven weeks at tenfold the complete-formula manganese concentration.
In that controlled sequence, marginal chlorosis intensified inward toward the midrib rather than remaining a single contact-burn spot.
Advanced controlled-study leaves became severely chlorotic, developed necrotic margins, and sometimes abscised.

Separate North Carolina field diagnostic observations described a different pathway of interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis; this supports a differential, not a universal visual signature.
Serial images from the same identified plant show a repeated lower- or older-leaf pattern across time rather than an isolated damaged leaflet.
A plausible manganese exposure or availability pathway is documented in fertilizer, stock solution, injector output, source water, substrate, soil, or persistently acidic root-zone conditions.
Correctly positioned leaf tissue and matched input or root-zone analysis demonstrate abnormal manganese status while competing nutrient and salinity explanations are evaluated.

Affected and unaffected plants map coherently to cultivar, fertigation zone, stock tank, substrate lot, pH treatment, or other measured exposure boundary rather than camera angle or chance distribution.
exclusions: Low substrate pH is present but manganese is not abnormally elevated and the pattern is better explained by direct acidic root stress; a 2025 hemp study did not produce toxic micronutrient accumulation from low pH alone under normal micronutrient rates.
Potassium deficiency better explains older-leaf serration and margin injury and is supported by tissue, feed, and root-zone evidence.
Boron toxicity or broad multi-ion salinity better explains the same older-leaf marginal chlorosis-to-necrosis sequence.
Magnesium deficiency produces a persistent interveinal pattern with stronger magnesium and root-zone evidence.
Drought, waterlogging, root hypoxia, root binding, temperature injury, or root disease explains the canopy pattern and washed-root findings.
Discrete expanding lesions, halos, surface growth, vascular discoloration, or laboratory results support a foliar, vascular, crown, or root pathogen.
Stippling, silver scars, webbing, eggs, mites, thrips, fecal spots, or another organism is confirmed on matched leaf surfaces.
Damage maps to spray droplets, residue, a lamp-facing surface, heat, airflow, abrasion, or another localized exposure rather than a root-mediated manganese pathway.
The change is limited to normal late-cycle senescence, stable cultivar pigmentation, or a camera white-balance, grow-light, glare, shadow, focus, or compression artifact.
A tissue result comes from a different cultivar, stage, organ, leaf age, plant, date, or laboratory method, or is contaminated by fertilizer dust or foliar micronutrient residue.

progression.description: Manganese supply, substrate pH, or root function may change before a reproducible leaf pattern appears; exposure history alone is not a positive visual label.
After seven weeks at tenfold manganese in one T1 silica-sand experiment, yellowing began along lower-leaf margins. This timing and dose are experiment-specific.
Marginal chlorosis intensified and moved inward toward the midrib while remaining nonspecific relative to potassium, boron, salinity, and root stress.

Controlled leaves developed necrotic margins, severe chlorosis, and occasional abscission; separate field observations described interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis rather than the same margin-first sequence.
Judge response from subsequent leaves, new-lesion rate, exposure records, root-zone measurements, and follow-up tissue results. Existing chlorosis, necrosis, and lost leaves will not recover.

lookAlikes: Acidic root-zone stress without manganese toxicity
Foliar spray or fertilizer contact injury
Spider-mite, broad-mite, hemp-russet-mite, or thrips injury
Cultivar pigmentation or camera color artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm manganese toxicity from marginal yellowing, interveinal yellowing, necrosis, one photograph, or one video; retain a suspected label until a measured manganese exposure and analytical evidence are linked to the imaged plant.

Capture serial whole-plant and matched upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views, leaves of known node and physiological age on both surfaces, margins and interveinal tissue, stems, inflorescences when present, washed roots, and the root zone under neutral repeatable lighting with scale and a healthy same-cultivar reference.

Record cultivar, propagation cohort, stage, days since onset, complete fertilizer formulation, manganese concentration and form, stock and injector calculations, source-water chemistry, substrate or soil lot, irrigation history, drainage, and any foliar or pesticide application.
Measure calibrated input and representative root-zone pH and EC, water content or container mass, drainage and oxygenation as appropriate; low pH alone does not establish manganese toxicity.

Submit a correctly positioned most-recently-mature-leaf sample plus matched symptomatic and healthy material and appropriate source-water, stock, final-solution, leachate, substrate, or soil samples to an agricultural laboratory; preserve plant, date, sample-position, method, units, and chain-of-custody links.

Interpret manganese with cultivar, stage, organ, laboratory method, pH, salinity, iron and other micronutrients; neither 47.88 mg/kg from the T1 treatment nor the 40–158 ppm North Carolina survey interval is a universal toxicity cutoff.

Inspect both leaf surfaces and washed roots with magnification and use a plant diagnostic laboratory when arthropods, foliar disease, vascular disease, root disease, viruses, viroids, or mixed disorders remain plausible; improvement after correction is supporting evidence, not retrospective ground truth.
immediateActions: Mark affected and matched healthy plants and preserve pre-correction serial images, fertilizer labels and batches, stock and injector records, source-water and root-zone measurements, washed roots, and representative tissue before changing the program.

Map affected plants against cultivar blocks, propagation cohorts, irrigation zones, stock tanks, substrate lots, pH measurements, spray events, and environmental gradients; isolate any suspected mixing or injector error.
Avoid blind flushing, liming, or micronutrient antagonism until salinity, root function, pH, and the actual manganese source are measured.
correctivePlan: Correct only a confirmed manganese source, formulation, injector, source-water, substrate, or root-zone pH problem using crop- and system-appropriate professional guidance.
Restore a balanced nutrient and pH program gradually while protecting drainage, oxygenation, and root function; do not chase one tissue value with an unmeasured antagonistic nutrient dose.

Track new leaves by node, new-lesion rate, roots, input and root-zone pH and EC, manganese exposure, and follow-up tissue results; reopen potassium, boron, magnesium, salinity, root, pathogen, arthropod, exposure, senescence, and imaging differentials if the expected response is absent.
prevention: Verify micronutrient formulation, stock-tank math, injector calibration, source-water contribution, substrate batch, and pH-meter calibration with recorded plant-group identifiers.
Trend input and root-zone pH and EC plus standardized most-recently-mature-leaf results by cultivar and stage instead of relying on one generic threshold or symptom chart.

Maintain same-cultivar healthy references, repeatable neutral-light imaging, defined leaf-position sampling, contamination controls, and change logs for fertilizer, water, substrate, sprays, and irrigation hardware.
warnings: The controlled T1 evidence used one cultivar, silica sand, and 180 micromolar manganese, tenfold the complete formula; its seven-week timing and margin-first sequence are not universal field thresholds.

Treated T1 foliage contained 47.88 mg/kg manganese, within the study-cited 41–93 mg/kg survey range, and dry weight did not differ significantly from controls; the authors called for higher-concentration work.
The North Carolina 40–158 ppm interval is the middle 50% of 6,119 floral-hemp survey submissions, not a causal toxicity cutoff and not a substitute for matched sampling and exposure evidence.

The 2025 pH-by-micronutrient study found reduced growth at pH 3.0–4.0 but no toxic accumulation under normal micronutrient rates, so acidic substrate cannot be converted directly into a manganese-toxicity label.

In that study, pH 3.8 plus four-times combined micronutrients produced lower-leaf toxicity symptoms in Sweetened but not Cherry Wine; the multi-element treatment does not isolate manganese and demonstrates cultivar dependence.

The published visual descriptions conflict: the controlled T1 study reported marginal injury while field observations reported interveinal injury, so either pathway requires human review and analytical confirmation.

The CC BY Figure 5 already stored under boron toxicity is a mixed-class composite with manganese in the left column and boron in the right; it is not duplicated or admitted as a clean manganese training sample.

The 2025 treatment figures combine pH, micronutrient rate, cultivar, and whole-plant response and are not indexed as manganese-specific media; this record intentionally remains without image or video ground truth.
All symptom-only, pH-only, unmatched, contaminated, method-unknown, multi-element, cultivar-unlinked, and analytically discordant samples require human review.

sources.title: Characterization of Nutrient Disorders of Cannabis sativa
supportedClaims: Single-element withholding in Cannabis sativa T1 documented boron deficiency, manganese toxicity, and the absence of a visible molybdenum-deficiency phenotype during the nine-week experiment.
Boron-deficient plants developed growing-tip stunting, distorted new leaves, marginal necrosis, death of growing tips, root-tip loss, and severe wilting in advanced stages.

Boron-withheld plants first showed slight whole-plant stunting from growing tips after six weeks; new and expanding leaflets were smaller and distorted, with bases narrower than tips, before margins became necrotic and leaves curled inward, downward, or at irregular angles.

At first boron-deficiency symptom expression, boron-withheld most-recent-mature leaves contained 2.46 mg/kg boron compared with 58.58 mg/kg in controls, 96% lower under the experiment conditions, and treated plants produced 28% less dry biomass.

Figure 4 is a CC BY 4.0 nine-panel composite: manganese, boron, and copper deficiency occupy the left, center, and right columns respectively, with initial, intermediate, and advanced rows; only the center column represents boron deficiency.

In Cannabis sativa T1, manganese-toxicity symptoms appeared seven weeks after treatment: marginal yellowing began on lower leaves, intensified inward toward the midrib, and advanced to marginal necrosis, severe chlorosis, and occasional leaf abscission.

The manganese-toxicity treatment used a tenfold increase over the complete formula (180 micromolar Mn versus 18 micromolar), but treated foliar Mn was 47.88 mg/kg, within the cited 41–93 mg/kg survey range; dry weight did not differ significantly from controls and the authors called for higher-concentration work to refine the threshold.
Figure 5 is a six-panel composite: manganese toxicity occupies the left column and boron toxicity the right, with initial, intermediate, and advanced symptom rows.

Molybdenum-withheld plants had foliar Mo 96% lower than controls yet developed no visual symptoms and no significant dry-weight difference by nine weeks, so a camera-visible Mo-deficiency phenotype was not established.
The experiment used one cultivar and complete withholding or tenfold treatments; tissue values and timing are experimental observations rather than universal Cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: North Carolina hemp diagnostic submissions included root binding, excess water, nutrient disorders, and herbicide injury as important abiotic differentials.

Root-bound transplants were commonly reported and affected plants did not reliably overcome the bound root system after field transplanting; secondary Fusarium and Pythium infections were also observed.
Clomazone carryover caused bleaching of newly formed hemp tissue in a documented commercial field case and the plants did not recover.

Field and diagnostic observations also documented manganese toxicity as interveinal yellowing followed by interveinal necrosis, supporting it as a real hemp differential but not a camera-only diagnosis.

sources.title: Hemp Leaf Tissue Nutrient Ranges: Refinement of Reference Standards for Floral Hemp
sources.publisher: North Carolina Cooperative Extension and North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
supportedClaims: The reference ranges were derived from 6,119 floral-hemp samples representing more than 100 varieties from field and greenhouse production in 76 North Carolina counties between 2017 and 2020.

For diagnostic hemp sampling, the publication recommends the most recently mature leaf, generally the third through fifth leaf below the growing point, using one or two leaves from 10 to 20 representative plants.
The adopted 40 to 158 ppm manganese interval represents the middle 50% of the survey submissions; it is a survey-derived sufficiency guide, not a causal toxicity cutoff.
The survey does not establish a universal manganese-toxicity threshold, and results require sampling-position, cultivar, stage, production-system, crop-purpose, and laboratory-method context.

sources.title: Impact of substrate pH and micronutrient fertility rates on Cannabis sativa
sources.publisher: Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America and the American Society of Agronomy
supportedClaims: In the first peat-perlite experiment, industrial-hemp shoot growth was reduced at substrate pH 3.0 or 4.0 relative to pH at or above 5.0; a separate mini-rhizotron experiment found inhibited root growth at very low pH. Those growth responses do not identify manganese toxicity by themselves.

Leaf micronutrient concentrations increased at the lowest pH, but the pH-rate experiments did not show toxic accumulation when micronutrients were supplied within normal production ranges, rejecting low substrate pH alone as sufficient evidence of manganese toxicity.

In the combined-rate experiment, Sweetened plants at pH 3.8 with four-times micronutrients developed lower-leaf micronutrient-toxicity symptoms, while Cherry Wine plants under the same treatment did not, demonstrating cultivar-dependent response.
The four-times treatment raised several micronutrients together rather than isolating manganese, so its visual response cannot be labeled as manganese-specific ground truth.

The study used BaOx, Cherry Wine, and Sweetened industrial-hemp cultivars in defined peat-perlite experiments; its pH values, rates, tissue results, symptoms, and root responses are not universal Cannabis thresholds.
The article is CC BY 4.0, but its treatment figures remain multi-factor, cultivar- and pH-specific context rather than clean manganese-toxicity training media.
